strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated problem: cold-start misrouting when the agent pool of an LLM-based MAS grows, supported by a clear motivating experiment (Figure 1) showing performance collapse under naive scale-up even with strong routers (Gemini-3-Pro drops from 60.6% to 52.7% on GAIA).

The method is concretely specified: agent-card-conditioned warm-up task synthesis (planner-executor-validator loop), evidence distillation from both success and failure traces into structured memory, a semantic trust region plus a KL trust-region surrogate (TRPO-style), and an explicit conservative fallback. The memory schema and full router/worker prompts are provided in appendices, aiding reproducibility.

The theoretical contribution, while simple, is correct and self-contained: the conservative lift (Eq. 6) plus non-interfering expansion (Assumption B.1) preserves performance (Lemma 4.2), and including the fallback memory in the feasible set (Eq. 9, Assumption B.2) yields the stage-wise monotonicity theorem (Thm 4.3). The proof in Appendix B is clean and easy to verify.

Experiments cover two benchmarks (GAIA, HLE-MCQ), three router backbones, pools from 3 to 10 agents, a deliberately malfunctioning agent pool, pass@3 baselines, and qualitative case studies (Appendix E) that trace concrete failure modes (cold-start misjudgment, brittle handover, confirmation bias) and how memory resolves them.

The discussion and impact statement are honest: the authors acknowledge the small pool scale (N ≤ 10), the retrieval-routing gap for million-scale Agentic Web settings, and security concerns such as malicious agents poisoning the evidence-collection process.
weaknesses: The monotonicity 'guarantee' is weaker than advertised. It essentially states that the system never does worse than not using the new agent (the fallback), which follows almost immediately from including the fallback in the feasible set. The substantive assumptions—non-interfering expansion, stationary task distribution, exact realizability of the lifted policy, and an exact expectation surrogate (Lemma 4.1 assumes J_k(π^k_m) is exactly L^k(m), which never holds empirically since the warm-up distribution only proxies D)—are strong and their gap from practice is not quantified.

Statistical rigor is lacking. GAIA validation has ~165 examples; headline differences (e.g., 47.27% vs 49.09% vs 51.15% across 5/7/10 agents) correspond to a handful of tasks. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, so the claim of 'strict monotonic improvement' at every step is fragile. Gains over naive scale-up at intermediate N (Figure 3) are also modest.

Missing ablations isolate the contribution poorly. There is no comparison against cheaper alternatives—e.g., warm-up with random or generic tasks, simply appending a richer agent description, or memory distilled only from successes. Thus it is unclear how much value comes from expansion-aware task customization versus any additional routing context or extra compute (~50 synthesized tasks × 4 parallel runs per expansion, whose cost is never analyzed).

The technical novelty is incremental: TRPO-style trust regions, conservative policy improvement, and natural-language memory modules for agents all exist; the novelty is mainly their combination and the expansion/cold-start framing. Related self-evolving MAS and memory work (ReasoningBank, MemRL, etc.) is cited but not empirically compared.

Evaluation scale is narrow: two benchmarks, pools of at most 10 hand-designed agents, and malfunctioning agents with hard-coded error strings rather than naturally arising unreliability. The gap between this setting and the motivating 'Agentic Web' scenario is acknowledged but not bridged, and no code release is stated, limiting reproducibility of the synthesis pipeline beyond the provided prompts.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and timely problem: router cold-start and performance degradation when new agents are added to an LLM-based multi-agent system. Figure 1 and the appendix case studies (Tables 4-6) provide concrete, interpretable illustrations of the failure mode.

The overall protocol (agent-conditioned warm-up task synthesis, distillation of success/failure evidence into auditable natural-language memory, and a conservative fallback that can disable the new agent) is a sensible engineering design, and the memory schema in Appendix D supports reproducibility of the setup.
The evaluation includes two benchmarks (GAIA and HLE-MCQ) and a genuinely useful robustness setting with intentionally malfunctioning agents, which is more adversarial than typical MAS evaluations.
The Discussion and Impact Statement are honest about scope limitations (pools of up to 10 agents only, not a complete safety solution) and the limitations are not hidden.
weaknesses: The headline theoretical contribution is essentially vacuous. The monotonicity 'guarantee' (Theorem 4.3) follows almost entirely from Assumption B.2: if you assume access to a fallback memory that exactly realizes the pre-expansion policy, and you only accept updates no worse than that fallback, performance cannot decrease — by construction. The TRPO-style KL trust region is not needed for the proof at all and appears decorative. Lemma 4.1 is a standard bandit identity, not a new result.

There is a large, unacknowledged theory-practice gap. The theorem assumes exact knowledge of J_k and exact advantages under the deployment distribution D, but in practice advantages are estimated from ~50 synthesized warm-up tasks drawn from D^warm, which the authors themselves admit is only a 'practical proxy' of D. The KL constraint between two LLM prompt-conditioned policies (Eq. 11) cannot be computed or verified in practice, and no empirical check is offered. The paper should either weaken the guarantee's claims or connect the theory to what is actually implemented.

The central empirical claim — that MonoScale outperforms strong-router baselines — is not supported by a fair comparison. MonoScale with 10 agents (55.15% GAIA) is compared against fixed 3-agent pools of strong routers, but Table 3 shows naive Gemini-3-Pro scale-up reaches 65.45% at 5 agents and 57.58% at 10 agents, both above MonoScale. The comparison conflates router strength with pool size, and the motivating 'performance collapse' phenomenon is cherry-picked: Table 3 shows naive scale-up often *improves* performance (DeepSeek +8.2%, Gemini +8.0% at 5 agents).

No statistical rigor. GAIA validation has only 165 tasks (53/53/26 per level); differences of 1-3 percentage points correspond to a handful of tasks. There are no error bars, no multiple seeds, and no significance tests, despite the paper's claims of 'strict monotonic improvement.' Indeed the level-wise results in Table 1 are visibly non-monotonic (Level 3: 26.92% -> 42.31% -> 30.77% -> 42.31%), so the 'monotonic' narrative holds only for the aggregate.

Missing ablations and sensitivity analyses: no ablation separating the contribution of task synthesis vs. memory updates vs. the conservative fallback, no sensitivity to the number of warm-up tasks (50), the trust-region parameter delta, or the memory budget K. Without these, it is impossible to know which component carries the gains.

Reproducibility is weak: no code or data release is mentioned, key hyperparameters (delta, K, the synthesizer model) are not specified, and the pipeline depends on proprietary models (GPT-5, Gemini-3-Pro) whose behavior may change. The appendix provides prompts but not the experimental configuration needed to reproduce the numbers.

The 'monotonic improvement' guarantee is empirically unsupported even in the paper's own results: Figure 3/Table 1 show the aggregate trend, but the guarantee concerns expected performance under D, which is never verified; and the noisy-pool results in Figure 4 show at best approximate stability, not a demonstrated guarantee.

Several claims are overstated relative to evidence, e.g., calling the result a 'verifiable lower-bound safety property' when nothing in the implementation is verifiable, and 'outperforming comparable strong baselines' when the strongest baseline (Gemini-3-Pro) is never compared at matched pool size with memory.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important problem—router cold-start and performance collapse under sequential agent-pool expansion—which is well motivated empirically (Figure 1 shows concrete degradation from 5 to 10 agents for DeepSeek-V3.2 and Qwen3).

The proposed mechanism is sensible and well-structured: agent-conditioned warm-up task synthesis (planner–executor–validator), distillation of both success and failure evidence into auditable natural-language memory, and a conservative fallback that can always revert to pre-expansion behavior. The auditable/rollbackable memory design is a nice practical touch.

The evaluation is comparatively thorough for this area: two benchmarks (GAIA, HLE-MCQ), strong proprietary-router baselines (GPT-5, Gemini-3-Pro, GPT-5.2), a noisy/malfunctioning agent pool setting with documented failure-mode injection (Appendix A.3), a pass@3 control (Figure 5), and three detailed case studies tracing failure and success trajectories (Appendix E).

The paper is clearly written, the contextual bandit formulation is clean, and the limitations are discussed honestly (restricted to pools of ≤10 agents, discussion of the retrieval-driven 'retrieve–route–calibrate' extension as future work, and a substantive impact statement covering memory poisoning and third-party agent risks).
weaknesses: The headline 'monotonic non-decreasing performance guarantee' (Theorem 4.3) is much weaker than advertised. The proof is essentially trivial: it holds by construction because the fallback candidate is always included in the feasible set and the argmax is assumed to be solved exactly (the fallback has zero surrogate loss improvement relative to itself). More importantly, the guarantee does not carry to the implemented system: (i) the surrogate (10)-(11) is estimated on synthetic warm-up samples Dwarm, treated as a proxy for the deployment distribution D, so the exact equality in Lemma 4.1 does not hold in practice; (ii) the expected KL trust region between two LLM policies induced by different memories cannot be computed exactly and no estimation procedure or value of δ is reported; (iii) candidate memory selection appears to be LLM-driven rather than an exact argmax over (11). The gap between theory and practice should be far more prominently acknowledged.

Statistical rigor is insufficient. GAIA's validation set is small (~165 tasks), so differences of a few percent correspond to a handful of tasks; the claim that the 10-agent MonoScale system (55.15%) is 'competitive with GPT-5 (54.55%)' rests on roughly one task. No confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple-seed/variance analysis are reported, despite stochastic LLM routing and 4-sample parallel execution. The HLE 'surpassing GPT-5' claim (19.90% vs 19.63%) is similarly fragile.

The 'strict monotonic improvement' claim is only true at the aggregate level; level-wise scores fluctuate substantially (e.g., GAIA L3: 26.92% → 42.31% → 30.77% → 42.31%), suggesting per-level non-monotonicity that the theory does not predict, which the text does not discuss.

Reproducibility gaps: the number of candidate memories, how Uk is concretely constructed and searched, the trust-region parameter δ, the token budget K, and the cost of the ~50-task familiarization per expansion are not reported. The correspondence between the warm-up distribution and the deployment distribution—critical for the surrogate to be meaningful—is described only qualitatively, and the method risks overfitting memory to the GAIA validation set.

Novelty is moderate: the components (memory-based agent improvement, safe-policy-improvement/trust-region logic from TRPO and conservative policy iteration, and data synthesis for probing) are existing techniques; the contribution is mainly their composition in the expansion setting. The formalization adds notation more than new insight, as the monotonicity result follows directly from including the identity/fallback candidate.

strengths: Identifies a real, practically relevant failure mode (cold-start misrouting during agent-pool expansion) and motivates it with concrete evidence (Figure 1 shows DeepSeek-V3.2 dropping from 0.558 to 0.491 and Qwen3 from 0.461 to 0.424 as the pool grows).

Clean problem formalization: sequential augmentation as contextual bandits with a conservative lift, giving a well-defined stage-wise monotonicity objective (Eq. 5) and an honest, clearly scoped guarantee (Theorem 4.3) with proofs in Appendix C.

Comprehensive empirical treatment: GAIA and HLE-MCQ evaluation, ablations (negative memory and customized warm-up both matter; removing negative memory drops 55.2%→40.0% at 10 agents), cross-router memory transfer, noisy/malfunctioning agent pool experiments, multi-seed variance assessment, onboarding cost analysis, and a candid error analysis of the non-monotonic dip at N=6 (Appendix D.7).

Theoretical assumptions are not just stated but empirically probed (Appendix C.2 validates non-interfering expansion via decision stability and reward stability tests), and the limitations section is genuinely substantive rather than perfunctory.
Strong safety/ethics discussion, including risks of memory poisoning by malicious agents, privacy in distilled memories, and explicit acknowledgment that the method is not a complete safety solution.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin relative to its billing. In the contextual bandit setting the surrogate (Lemma 4.1) is exact, so any candidate achieving higher surrogate value genuinely improves J; the trust-region/KL constraint plays no role in the proof (the fallback has KL = 0 and wins by construction via Assumption C.2). The monotonicity result is thus close to trivial given the assumption that a no-op option is always in the feasible set. Moreover, the deployment procedure (Appendix B) performs one-shot selection over a finite candidate set and does not actually optimize the constrained objective, and it is unclear how the KL constraint (Eq. 11) is ever computed or enforced in practice.

Headline comparisons are somewhat overstated. The main claim that a 10-agent MonoScale system (55.15%) 'outperforms strong baselines' holds only against 3-agent fixed pools; Table 3 shows DeepSeek-V3.2 at 5 agents (55.76%) and Gemini-3-Pro at 5 agents (65.45%) exceed MonoScale's best. The authors' justification (a-priori predictability of the operating point) is reasonable but the framing shifts the comparison in the method's favor, and the papers' claims should be stated more carefully.

The non-interfering expansion assumption is strong (legacy-plan rewards are provably unchanged), yet its empirical validation is limited: 100 HLE samples with a 19/100 vs 21/100 difference, and a decision-stability check on one system. This is acknowledged, but the guarantee's practical scope remains narrow.

No analysis of the warm-up distribution mismatch: Dwarm_k is treated as a proxy for the deployment distribution D, but the effect of this distribution shift on the validity of the surrogate estimates and candidate selection is never quantified.

Scale and statistical rigor are limited: main results appear single-seed on a 165-question GAIA validation set (differences of 1–2 points are within reported seed variance of ~1.4–2.9 points on a 40-task subset), pools only reach 10 agents (20-agent probe on HLE only), and some component-level results are non-monotonic (e.g., MonoScale Level 3 at 7 agents is 30.77% vs 46.15% naive).

Reproducibility is partial: the code link is given only as 'here' with no resolvable URL in the manuscript, and key implementation details (how candidate memories are ranked, how the semantic trust region is implemented as an LLM check) are described only at a high level, which would make exact replication difficult despite the detailed prompts in Appendix A.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and underexplored problem—cold-start performance collapse when expanding LLM-based multi-agent systems—and the motivating experiments (Figure 1, Table 3) provide concrete evidence that naive scale-up is non-monotonic even for strong routers like Gemini-3-Pro.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: ablations of both negative memory and customized warm-up (Table 4), a cross-router memory transfer study (Table 5), scaling beyond 10 agents (D.4), onboarding cost analysis (D.5), multi-seed variance (D.6), error analysis of the local dip at N=6 (D.7), noisy-pool experiments (D.8), and detailed qualitative case studies (Appendix F) tracing specific failure modes.

The method is well-motivated and practical: agent-conditioned familiarization tasks, distillation of both success and failure evidence into auditable/rollbackable natural-language memory, and a conservative fallback that always preserves pre-expansion behavior are sensible, deployable design choices.
Limitations are discussed honestly and at length (conditional nature of the guarantee, memory token budget, small pool sizes), and the paper does not overclaim universal monotonicity.
Reproducibility support is decent: full prompts, agent configurations, malfunctioning-agent specifications, and the algorithm are all included, with code released.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is largely tautological. Lemma 4.1 is the standard exact TRPO identity specialized to bandits (where no approximation is needed), and Theorem 4.3's monotonicity follows almost immediately from the fact that the conservative fallback is included in the feasible set by construction. The 'guarantee' essentially restates that an argmax over a set containing the baseline cannot do worse than the baseline—a point rarely worthy of theorem status.

There is a significant gap between the theory and the deployed method. Equations (11)/(16) select the memory by argmax over the true expected objective J under the deployment distribution D, but Algorithm 1 selects based on finite rollouts over a synthesized warm-up distribution D^warm that is only a 'practical proxy' of D. The theorem therefore does not actually certify the implemented procedure, and the trust-region/KL constraint is acknowledged (Appendix B) to be analytical window dressing rather than an enforced mechanism.

The headline comparisons are framed favorably. Table 3 shows that naive scale-up with DeepSeek-V3.2 and Gemini-3-Pro actually improves at 5 agents (+8.2% and +8.0%), and Gemini-3-Pro at 5 agents (65.45%) substantially exceeds MonoScale's best result (55.15%). The paper's justification for benchmarking against fixed 3-agent pools (Section 6) is a reasonable argument about a-priori predictability, but the abstract's claim of 'outperforming strong-router fixed-pool baselines' elides that stronger configurations of the baselines exist.

Statistical rigor is thin for the central claims. Main results appear to be single-seed point estimates on the 165-question GAIA validation set; the variance study is on a 40-task subset with three seeds, and several reported margins (e.g., the N=6 dip of ~1.2 points, 2.89-point standard deviations on 40 tasks) are of comparable magnitude to differences being interpreted.

The evaluation scope is narrow relative to the framing: only two benchmarks, pools of at most 10 agents (one 20-agent probe), and warm-up task synthesis that may correlate with the benchmark distribution, raising potential concerns about how much of the gain reflects genuine agent profiling versus distributional overlap.

Practical memory updates rely on LLM-based distillation with heuristic 'semantic trust region' filtering; no evidence is provided that the distilled candidates actually satisfy the KL constraint or that the candidate-selection step reliably improves the true objective rather than overfitting the warm-up set.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely problem: cold-start performance collapse when scaling up agent pools in LLM-based multi-agent systems. The motivating evidence (Figure 1, Table 3) clearly demonstrates the failure mode across multiple router backbones, including strong proprietary ones.

The experimental work is relatively thorough for this area: matched w/ and w/o memory comparisons at each scale, an ablation isolating negative memory vs. customized warm-up (Table 4), a cross-router memory transfer study (Table 5), a multi-seed variance analysis (D.6), onboarding cost analysis (D.5), and detailed case studies (Appendix F). The ablation result that removing negative memory causes a drop from 55.2% to 40.0% at 10 agents is a compelling attribution of where the gains come from.

The authors are notably honest about limitations: they explicitly state the monotonicity guarantee is conditional, empirically test the non-interfering expansion assumption (Appendix C.2), explain the local dip at N=6 with a concrete root-cause analysis (D.7), and openly justify their baseline-comparison strategy (fixed 3-agent strong-router pools) rather than hiding it.

The presentation is clear: the contextual-bandit formalization, conservative lift, fallback mechanism, and trust-region selection are well-motivated, and Algorithm 1 plus the memory schema in Appendix E support reproducibility. Code is released.
The combination of auditable, rollbackable natural-language memory with a conservative fallback is a practical and sensible design that many practitioners could build on.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is modest and the theory-practice gap is significant. Theorem 4.3 essentially re-derives TRPO-style conservative policy improvement in the contextual-bandit case, where the surrogate is exact, so the result is close to trivial once the fallback exists. More importantly, the deployed algorithm (Algorithm 1) never computes the KL trust region or the advantage-weighted surrogate; the 'trust region' is implemented as an LLM-based semantic consistency check plus candidate filtering. The theorem is thus a 'theoretical lens' whose assumptions are only approximately connected to what actually runs, and the paper itself concedes this (Appendix B).

The baseline comparison has a fairness concern that somewhat weakens the headline claims. Table 3 shows Gemini-3-Pro naive scale-up reaching 65.45% at 5 agents, exceeding MonoScale's best (55.15%). The paper's justification (predictability asymmetry, a-priori knowable operating point) is reasonable but means the 'competitive with SOTA' claim rests on comparing against fixed small-pool configurations rather than the best achievable baseline configuration.

The scale of validation is limited: GAIA validation has only 165 questions (observed std ~1.4–2.9 points on a 40-task subset), so per-point gains of 2–3 points at intermediate scales (e.g., 5 vs. 7 agents) are marginal, and the pool size caps at 10 (20 in one appendix probe). The claimed 'monotonic improvement' is empirically only a trend, which the paper acknowledges in D.6, but the framing in the abstract and title ('monotonic improvement') is stronger than the evidence.

The assumption that the warm-up distribution Dwarm is a faithful proxy for the deployment distribution D is under-examined; the validator's requirement of deterministic, executable solutions may systematically bias the synthesized tasks away from realistic failure modes, and the D.7 analysis (budget-exhaustion failures not covered by warm-up) suggests this proxy gap is real.

Novelty is incremental: the ingredients (memory-based agent learning, conservative policy updates, contextual-bandit routing) are all established; the contribution is primarily their combination and problem framing rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Several empirical numbers lack error bars or significance testing in the main text (e.g., HLE gains in Table 2), making it hard to judge whether intermediate gains are distinguishable from run-to-run variance.
